A leveraged fund delivers a multiple of an index’s daily return. A haircut is the discount a lender or regulator applies to a security’s value when counting it as collateral or capital.

Formally. Leverage is gross exposure over equity, \(\sum_i |x_i|/W\), and a levered book’s VaR as a fraction of equity is the leverage times the unlevered fraction. For a long position bought with an initial equity fraction \(e_0\) and a maintenance requirement \(m\) on equity over market value, a margin call comes after a fall in price of

\[ 1 - \frac{1 - e_0}{1 - m} , \]

one third for the common US combination of half the purchase borrowed, the Regulation T initial requirement, and FINRA’s 25% maintenance minimum. Divided by the daily volatility, that is the answer to §13.6’s question of what market move triggers a margin call. A clearing house’s initial margin is a VaR or ES of the account’s loss over a close-out period of several days, at a confidence level of 99% or more, while variation margin settles each day’s P&L in cash. CME’s SPAN instead charges the worst loss over a fixed grid of price and volatility scenarios, and ISDA’s SIMM, for uncleared trades between dealers, aggregates sensitivities with prescribed risk weights and correlations calibrated to a 99% ten-day loss. A clearing house’s default fund, pooled among its members, covers losses beyond a defaulter’s margin and is sized by stress scenarios rather than by a VaR.

Why it appears here. §1.7 distinguishes margin from VaR and notes that the maximum loss on a short position is unbounded; §3.1 describes the SEC’s 1980 move to statistically based haircuts; §9.3 has prime brokers, the brokers that finance hedge funds, setting margin from their own models; and §9.4 describes clearing-house margin, SPAN and SIMM, and Regulation T and portfolio-margin accounts for individuals. §13.6 asks what move triggers a margin call, §13.1 lists margin and leveraged funds among the retail exposures VaR handles worst, and §6.11 names clearing-house default funds among the uses of extreme value theory.

Deeper. CPMI–IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (Bank for International Settlements, 2012), principles 4 and 6, on credit risk and margin at clearing houses. The Federal Reserve’s Regulation T (12 CFR Part 220) and FINRA Rule 4210, for the retail rules.

Part V — Practice, regulation and evaluation. The last part covers how VaR is used and judged: the sizing and performance vocabulary of §8 and §13, the rules of §9, and the discipline that keeps a backtest honest. Several entries are about institutions rather than mathematics, and their formal sections state rules rather than theorems.

A.43 Stops, gaps, average true range and sizing rules

The idea. Many traders control risk trade by trade. They decide in advance the price at which they will exit a losing position, and size the position so that the loss at that price is a fixed fraction of equity. The exit is usually a stop order, an instruction to sell once the market trades at or through a given price. A stop does not guarantee that price. It becomes an order to sell at the next available price, and when the market gaps — opens far below the previous close, or trades through the level in a halt or a rush — the fill can land well beyond the stop. The difference is slippage. Volatility-scaled stops set the exit at a multiple of a recent range measure, most often the average true range, which makes the rule a volatility-based sizing rule in disguise. A rebalancing band is the analogous device for a risk budget: act only when a quantity drifts outside a band, then trade back toward the target.

Formally. Fixed-fractional sizing sets the position at \(x_i = B_iW/d_i\), with \(d_i\) the distance to the stop as a fraction of the price, so the planned loss at the stop is \(B_iW\). The true range of a day is

\[ \max\big(\text{high}_t - \text{low}_t,\ |\text{high}_t - \text{close}_{t-1}|,\ |\text{low}_t - \text{close}_{t-1}|\big), \]

which counts an overnight gap as part of the day’s range, and the average true range (ATR) is its moving average, conventionally over fourteen days. If the stop is set at \(c\) ATRs and the ATR is roughly proportional to \(\sigma_i\), then \(d_i \propto \sigma_i\) and the rule becomes \(x_i \propto B_iW/\sigma_i\): the VaR budget of §13.3 with a different constant in place of \(k_{0.95}\). Summing the \(B_i\) over open positions, sometimes called portfolio heat, adds risks while ignoring correlation. A band rule acts when utilisation, the VaR divided by its budget, exceeds an upper limit such as 1.25, and then trades back to 1.

Why it appears here. §13.3 shows that a VaR budget, a volatility target and volatility-scaled stop sizing are one rule, and lists where VaR adds to stops: gaps, correlation, and holdings managed without stops. §8.2 marks the claim that a fixed-fraction stop caps the loss as a heuristic, because “gaps and halts go through it”. The flowchart of §13.2, §13.3 and §14.4 all use a 125% band.

Deeper. Trend-Following in Financial Markets, sec. 8.5 on position sizing and sec. 11.3 on stops. Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (Trend Research, 1978), where the average true range originates.

A.44 The Sharpe ratio, factor portfolios and volatility management

The idea. The Sharpe ratio is return per unit of risk: average excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by volatility. Leverage does not change it, so it ranks strategies rather than position sizes. A factor portfolio is built to isolate one source of return: the market as a whole, or a long-short bet on a characteristic such as value or momentum. The Kenneth French data library publishes the returns of many such portfolios, and of industry portfolios, for US stocks from 1926; a value-weighted portfolio holds each stock in proportion to its market capitalisation. Volatility targeting scales exposure so that forecast volatility stays constant, holding more when markets are calm and less when they are violent. Moreira and Muir’s volatility-managed portfolios scale by the inverse of recent variance rather than of volatility, a more aggressive version of the same idea. Both are a VaR budget under another name.

Formally. For a risk-free rate \(r_f\), the Sharpe ratio is \(\mathrm{SR} = E[r - r_f]/\operatorname{sd}(r - r_f)\), annualised from daily data by \(\sqrt{252}\) under IID returns. Volatility targeting holds the exposure multiple \(\sigma^\star/\sigma_t\) for a target \(\sigma^\star\), so the scaled position’s forecast volatility is \(\sigma^\star\) every day. A one-day 95% VaR budget \(B\) is the daily target \(\sigma^\star = B/k_{0.95}\) (§8.2), which in the normal case is \(\sqrt{252}\,B/1.645 = 9.65B\) a year. Moreira and Muir’s managed factor return is the factor’s return times \(c/\hat\sigma_t^2\), with \(\hat\sigma_t^2\) the previous month’s realised variance and \(c\) a constant that matches the unmanaged factor’s volatility, so exposure falls in proportion to variance rather than to volatility.

Why it appears here. The front matter’s value-weighted market and industry portfolios come from the French library. §8.2 shows that a VaR budget and a volatility target are the same rule, a 1% budget being a 9.65% annual target, and §13.3 uses it for sizing. §11.6 cites Moreira and Muir’s finding that inverse-variance scaling raised Sharpe ratios for the market and many factor portfolios, and Cederburg and co-authors’ challenge to it out of sample.

Deeper. Moreira & Muir (2017) and Cederburg, O’Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020), in §4.6. Sharpe, “The Sharpe Ratio,” Journal of Portfolio Management 21(1) (1994), 49–58. The Kenneth R. French data library, and Trend-Following in Financial Markets, sec. 11.2, on volatility targeting.

A.45 Benchmarks, active return and tracking error

The idea. An active manager is judged against a benchmark, usually an index, and the relevant risk is not of losing money but of trailing it. Active return is the portfolio’s return minus the benchmark’s, and tracking error is its volatility. A manager running 3% tracking error, with normal active returns, expects to land within three percentage points of the index in about two years out of three. Because tracking error is a volatility, a VaR of the active return is a multiple of it, and an active manager’s risk budget is a tracking-error budget. The information ratio, mean active return divided by tracking error, is the active manager’s Sharpe ratio.

Formally. With portfolio weights \(w\) and benchmark weights \(w_b\), the active weights are \(w - w_b\), and the ex-ante tracking error is \(\sqrt{(w - w_b)'\Sigma(w - w_b)}\), annualised by \(\sqrt{252}\) from a daily \(\Sigma\). Under normality, with the mean dropped, the relative VaR of §7.3 is \(z_\alpha\) times the tracking error times \(V\). The information ratio is \(E[r_p - r_b]/\operatorname{sd}(r_p - r_b)\) for portfolio and benchmark returns \(r_p\) and \(r_b\).

Why it appears here. §7.3 defines relative and tracking-error VaR, and §9.2 describes the tracking-error budget as a relative VaR in volatility units; §8.4 separates the three meanings of “relative VaR”, of which this is one.

Deeper. Grinold & Kahn, Active Portfolio Management, 2nd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 1999). Roll, “A Mean/Variance Analysis of Tracking Error,” Journal of Portfolio Management 18(4) (1992), 13–22.

A.46 Drawdowns, the drawdown of a random walk, and sequence risk

The idea. A drawdown is the fall from the highest value reached so far to the current value, and the maximum drawdown is the worst such fall over a period. It is a path property: it depends on the order in which gains and losses arrive and it accumulates over many steps, which is why investors feel it and why a one-step measure like VaR does not describe it. A random walk has drawdowns too, and probability theory gives their typical size: the expected maximum drawdown grows with the square root of time, with a constant that ties it to the daily volatility. Sequence-of-returns risk is the same dependence on order, seen by someone adding or withdrawing money: with withdrawals, losses early in a retirement do more damage than the same losses late, even when the average return is identical.

Formally. For an account’s equity \(W_t\), the drawdown at \(t\) is \(1 - W_t/\max_{s \le t} W_s\), and the maximum drawdown over a period is its largest value. For a Brownian motion with no drift and volatility \(\sigma\) per day, the expected maximum drawdown over \(h\) days is

\[ \sqrt{\pi/2}\;\sigma\sqrt h \;\approx\; 1.25\,\sigma\sqrt h , \]

and positive drift lowers it. Without cash flows, terminal wealth \(W_0\prod_t(1 + r_t)\) does not depend on the order of the returns. With a withdrawal \(c\) each period, \(W_t = (W_{t-1} - c)(1 + r_t)\), and it does: the same returns in a different order give a different ending balance, because an early loss shrinks the base on which every later gain works.

Why it appears here. §1.7 contrasts drawdown with VaR, and §7.7 defines conditional drawdown at risk, the ES of drawdowns. §9.3’s multi-manager platforms cut capital at drawdown thresholds. §13.5 tabulates US drawdowns as multiples of daily VaR and checks them against this result, about twelve daily 95% VaRs over a year, and §13.7 names sequence risk as something a one-day quantile cannot see.

Deeper. Magdon-Ismail, Atiya, Pratap & Abu-Mostafa (2004) and Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin (2005), in §4.6. Bengen, “Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Historical Data,” Journal of Financial Planning 7(4) (1994), on sequence risk in retirement. Trend-Following in Financial Markets, sec. 11.4, on drawdown control.

A.47 Bank capital and the Basel internal-models approach

The idea. Regulatory capital is the equity a bank must hold so that it can absorb losses without failing. For market risk, the losses on the trading book of positions held to trade rather than to keep, the 1996 Basel amendment let large banks compute the charge from their own VaR models, subject to standards, instead of using fixed regulatory percentages. The bargain had two parts. The model’s number was multiplied by at least three, a safety factor for everything the model leaves out. And the model was backtested daily against the bank’s P&L, with a penalty for too many breaches: the traffic light raises the multiplier from three toward four as exceptions accumulate. After the crisis, Basel 2.5 added a second VaR computed on a stressed year, so that a calm period could not drive capital down. A bank’s own estimate of the capital it needs, usually at a higher confidence level, is economic capital, a separate number from the regulatory one.

Formally. Under the 1996 rules the daily charge is the first term below, with VaR at 99% over ten days and \(\overline{\operatorname{VaR}}_{60}\) its average over the last sixty business days; Basel 2.5 adds the second, the same expression for stressed VaR:

\[ \max\big(\operatorname{VaR}_{t-1},\ m_c\,\overline{\operatorname{VaR}}_{60}\big) + \max\big(\operatorname{sVaR}_{t-1},\ m_s\,\overline{\operatorname{sVaR}}_{60}\big). \]

\(m_c\) is three plus a plus factor set by the traffic light (§12.4), 0 for four or fewer exceptions in 250 days and rising to 1 for ten or more; \(m_s\) is also at least three. The backtest compares each day’s VaR with that day’s P&L in two forms: hypothetical P&L, the change in value of the previous evening’s positions held fixed, which is what the VaR forecasts; and actual P&L, the result actually booked, which also reflects intraday trading and new positions.

Why it appears here. §1.7 says regulators set capital “as a multiple of VaR”, and §2.1’s ten-day 99% row is this rule’s convention. §3.3 and §9.1 describe the 1996 amendment and its capital formula; §12.4 sets out the traffic light and its error rates; §3.5, §7.4 and §9.1 describe stressed VaR; and §10.2 and §12.8 distinguish hypothetical from actual P&L. §6.11’s economic capital is the internal counterpart.

Deeper. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (1996a, 1996b, 2009), in §4.1; the 1996b backtesting framework is short and a model of how to write a statistical rule. Jorion (2006), in §4.7, for how the rules work in practice.

A.48 The Fundamental Review of the Trading Book

The idea. The FRTB is the post-crisis rewrite of bank market-risk capital, finalised in 2019. It keeps the internal-model architecture of A.47 but changes most of its parts. The capital measure moves from 99% VaR to 97.5% expected shortfall, so that the size of tail losses counts. It is calibrated to a period of stress rather than to recent data. Horizons stretch from a uniform ten days to between ten and 120 days, according to how quickly each risk factor could be traded out of. And approval moves from the bank to the trading desk: each desk keeps its model only while it passes two tests, a backtest of its one-day VaR and a profit-and-loss attribution test checking that the risk model’s view of the desk’s P&L matches the desk’s own pricing.

Formally. With a base horizon of ten days and liquidity horizons \(\mathrm{LH}_j \in \{10, 20, 40, 60, 120\}\) days, the liquidity-adjusted ES is a nested square-root-of-time rule,

\[ \operatorname{ES} = \sqrt{\operatorname{ES}_{10}(P)^2 + \sum_{j \ge 2}\Big(\operatorname{ES}_{10}(P, j) \sqrt{\tfrac{\mathrm{LH}_j - \mathrm{LH}_{j-1}}{10}}\Big)^{2}}, \]

where, at the 97.5% level, \(\operatorname{ES}_{10}(P)\) is the ten-day ES of the portfolio \(P\) with all its risk factors shocked, and \(\operatorname{ES}_{10}(P, j)\) the same with only the factors whose liquidity horizon is at least \(\mathrm{LH}_j\) shocked. The ES is computed on a reduced set of factors over the worst twelve-month stress period, then scaled by the ratio of full-set to reduced-set ES in current data. Desk-level backtesting counts exceptions of one-day VaR at 99% and 97.5% over the last 250 days, and the attribution test compares the risk model’s P&L with hypothetical P&L using a rank correlation and a distributional distance.

Why it appears here. §3.5 and §9.1 describe the move to 97.5% ES, the stress calibration and the desk-level tests; §5.6 explains the choice of 97.5%, which matches 99% VaR for a normal distribution; and §7.5 lists the liquidity horizons. After §5.4 and §11.5 the formula deserves a second look: the regulation that retired VaR still builds its long horizons by square-root-of-time scaling.

Deeper. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2019), in §4.1: the standard itself, which contains the formula above.

A.49 Fund and insurance rules: UCITS, Rule 18f-4 and Solvency II

The idea. VaR has become a standard way to cap the leverage of investment funds that use derivatives, because one rule can then apply to very different funds. A European UCITS fund — the EU framework for funds sold to the public — that uses derivatives in a sophisticated way must measure its global exposure by VaR and keep it under one of two caps: an absolute cap, a percentage of its net asset value, or a relative cap, a multiple of the VaR of a reference portfolio without derivatives. The US adopted the same design for registered funds in Rule 18f-4. European insurers face a different VaR rule: under Solvency II their capital must cover a one-in-two-hundred-year fall in their own funds, the excess of assets over liabilities, over one year.

Formally. UCITS (CESR, 2010): 99% confidence, a twenty-day horizon and at least one year of data, with absolute VaR at most 20% of net asset value or relative VaR at most twice the reference portfolio’s. Funds with simpler derivative use apply the commitment approach instead, which converts each derivative into an equivalent position in its underlying. Rule 18f-4 (Securities and Exchange Commission, 2020, in force from 2022): 99% over twenty trading days and at least three years of data, with VaR at most 200% of a designated reference portfolio’s, an unleveraged index reflecting the fund’s markets, or 20% of net assets where no suitable index exists; funds with limited derivatives exposure are exempt from the VaR test. Solvency II: the solvency capital requirement is the 99.5% one-year VaR of basic own funds. A fund’s net asset value is its assets minus its liabilities.

Why it appears here. §2.1’s twenty-day and one-year rows are these conventions, and §3.6 dates them. §7.3 and §8.4 contrast the regulatory “relative VaR”, a ratio to a reference portfolio’s VaR, with the asset manager’s, and §9.2 sets out all three regimes.

Deeper. CESR (2010) and Securities and Exchange Commission (2020), in §4.1. Directive 2009/138/EC (Solvency II), article 101, for the 99.5% calibration.

A.50 Model risk and independent model validation

The idea. Model risk is the risk of loss from decisions based on a model that is wrong or misused: wrong in its specification, wrong in its implementation, or right but applied outside the conditions it was built for. VaR carries all three. Reasonable methods disagree by large factors on the same book, implementations of the same method disagree, and a model calibrated on calm data gets applied to a crisis. A further form appears once a number drives limits and pay: the incentive to change the model rather than the risk, an instance of Goodhart’s law that a measure made into a target stops measuring what it did. The institutional answer is independent validation: people with no stake in the model’s output review its design, test its implementation and its outcomes, and can stop its use.

Formally. US supervisory guidance (SR 11-7) defines a model as a quantitative method that turns input data into estimates using statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theory, and model risk as the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. It asks for effective challenge and sets out three elements of validation: evaluation of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis, of which backtesting is the main instance for VaR. Implementation risk, the same specification coded differently, is part of model risk, and is tested by independent reimplementation and by invariance checks such as §14.5’s.

Why it appears here. §1.3 warns that two competent teams routinely differ by tens of percent, and §11.3 quantifies the disagreement with Beder’s and Marshall and Siegel’s results. §3.4 makes LTCM “the standard case study for model risk”; §11.7 documents the London Whale’s model change and names independent validation as the defence; and §14.5’s four checks are a minimal validation for a personal system.

Deeper. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, SR 11-7 (2011). Beder (1995) and Marshall & Siegel (1997), in §4.5.

A.51 Backtest hygiene: look-ahead, overfitting and data

The idea. A backtest is evidence only if each forecast could have been made at the time, from data available then, by a method chosen before the test. Look-ahead bias breaks the first condition: a forecast that uses later data, even indirectly through a parameter fitted on the whole sample, looks better than any real forecast could. Overfitting, or data snooping, breaks the second: try enough variants on the same data and the best will look good by luck. The remedies are to choose the method on one period and judge it on another it never saw, which is out-of-sample testing, and to count every variant tried. Two data problems are as common as the statistical ones. Prices must be adjusted for dividends and splits, or the return series contains false crashes at every split and misses the income from every payout. And a holding with a short history needs a proxy, whose differences from the real thing become an unmeasured risk.

Formally. A forecast for day \(t\) may depend only on \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\) (A.4), and that includes its parameters, its window and the choice of model. If \(M\) variants are tried on the same data, the best of their test statistics is biased upward: for independent standard normal statistics the expected maximum is about 2.5 for a hundred variants and grows like \(\sqrt{2\ln M}\), and the bar for significance should rise with it. A split-adjusted series divides every price before an \(n\)-for-one split by \(n\), and a total-return series reinvests each dividend on the day the stock starts trading without it, so that \(S_t/S_{t-1} - 1\) computed from the series is the holder’s actual return. An unadjusted two-for-one split appears as a return of \(-50\%\).

Why it appears here. §6.1 requires every backtested forecast to use “only data available the evening before”; §12.1 and §12.8 forbid refitting on the full sample and tuning the EWMA decay on the period then reported. §14.1 asks for prices adjusted for dividends and splits and a documented proxy for short histories, §14.5’s first check exists to catch unadjusted prices, and §11.7 shows proxies hiding risk.

Deeper. White, “A Reality Check for Data Snooping,” Econometrica 68(5) (2000), 1097–1126. Foundations of Econometrics, sec. 9.7, “Backtests are econometrics”. Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, “Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism,” Notices of the AMS 61(5) (2014), 458–471, on backtest overfitting.
